A study published in Virology Journal by Zhezhe Tian and colleagues at Qilu Hospital of Shandong University now adds an epigenetic dimension to how physicians might gauge that inflammatory damage. The researchers report that methylation of the promoter region of CXCL16, a gene encoding a chemokine implicated in hepatic injury, is significantly reduced in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, and that this hypomethylation tracks closely with the intensity of inflammation in the liver. The work, conducted at the Department of Hepatology of Qilu Hospital and the Institute of Hepatology of Shandong University, was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and approved by the hospital’s Medical Ethical Committee in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The biological logic behind the study rests on a well-established principle of gene regulation. DNA methylation, the addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases within gene promoter regions, generally acts as a brake on transcription. When a promoter is heavily methylated, the chromatin adopts a closed configuration that limits access of transcriptional machinery, and the downstream gene is expressed at low levels. Conversely, loss of methylation, known as hypomethylation, often permits increased gene expression. For chemokines, which are potent signalling molecules that recruit immune cells to sites of infection or damage, the methylation state of the promoter can therefore dictate how strongly an inflammatory signal is broadcast. CXCL16, or C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 16, is one such chemokine, recognized as a key mediator in liver injury, yet its epigenetic regulation in chronic hepatitis B had remained unclear prior to this investigation. To address that gap, the team assembled a study population of 217 patients with chronic hepatitis B, subdivided into 113 who were positive for hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and 104 who were HBeAg-negative, alongside 27 healthy controls. HBeAg status is a clinically meaningful marker in HBV infection: HBeAg-positive patients are typically considered to carry a higher viral replicative activity and a distinct immunological profile compared with those who have seroconverted. By stratifying patients this way, the researchers could ask whether epigenetic changes at the CXCL16 promoter differed not only between diseased and healthy livers, but also between the two major immunological phases of chronic infection. Across three molecular layers, the same pattern emerged. First, the percentage of methylation reference, a quantitative measure of promoter methylation, was significantly lower in chronic hepatitis B patients than in healthy controls, and the reduction was especially pronounced in HBeAg-positive cases. Second, mRNA levels of CXCL16 were markedly higher in the patient groups, again most prominently among those who were HBeAg-positive. Third, serum concentrations of the CXCL16 protein were elevated in patients relative to controls. The concordance across methylation, transcript and protein measurements is what gives the finding its mechanistic weight, because it suggests a coherent pathway from epigenetic derepression to enhanced chemokine production rather than an isolated correlation at a single molecular level. The inverse relationship between methylation and expression was borne out statistically. CXCL16 promoter methylation was negatively correlated with CXCL16 expression, which is precisely what promoter methylation biology would predict: the less the promoter is methylated, the more the gene is transcribed and translated. Notably, methylation also showed negative correlations with several clinical and immunological markers. These included HBeAg status itself, the liver injury enzymes alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and the pro-inflammatory cytokines tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). In practical terms, patients with the lowest CXCL16 promoter methylation tended to have the highest levels of transaminases, the canonical blood markers of hepatocyte damage, and the highest circulating concentrations of inflammatory cytokines that drive and amplify hepatic inflammation. ALT and AST are enzymes released when hepatocytes are injured, and their serum activities form the backbone of non-invasive monitoring in viral hepatitis. TNF-α and IL-1β, meanwhile, are central cytokines in the innate immune response, capable of activating hepatic stellate cells, promoting leukocyte recruitment and sustaining the inflammatory milieu that, over years, leads to fibrosis and malignant transformation. The observation that CXCL16 promoter methylation aligns with all of these parameters simultaneously positions the epigenetic mark as a potential integrator of inflammatory burden. Rather than reflecting a single laboratory value, hypomethylation appears to sit upstream of a network of destructive processes in the HBV-infected liver. To test whether the methylation measurement could do more than describe associations, the researchers performed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, a standard method for evaluating the discriminative capacity of a biomarker. The analysis demonstrated that CXCL16 promoter methylation had a favourable ability to distinguish HBeAg-positive patients, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.749. An AUC of 0.5 would indicate performance no better than chance, while 1.0 would indicate perfect discrimination, so a value of 0.749 represents a moderate-to-good level of diagnostic accuracy. Taken together with the significant correlations with inflammatory markers, the authors suggest that CXCL16 promoter methylation could serve as a complementary indicator for identifying chronic hepatitis B patients who carry a higher inflammatory burden. The clinical appeal of such a marker lies in its non-invasive character. Assessing liver inflammation today often relies on serum transaminases, which can fluctuate and normalise even in the presence of ongoing disease, or on liver biopsy, which remains the gold standard for grading inflammation and staging fibrosis but carries procedural risks, sampling variability and patient reluctance. A blood-based epigenetic measurement that reflects the regulatory state of a chemokine gene could, if validated further, offer a repeatable and safer window into hepatic inflammatory activity. The authors conclude that CXCL16 promoter hypomethylation is closely associated with elevated CXCL16 expression and exacerbated hepatic inflammation in chronic hepatitis B patients, and propose it as a potential non-invasive biomarker for assessing CHB-related liver inflammation. Beyond its diagnostic promise, the study enriches the mechanistic picture of how HBV infection translates into chronic liver damage. Viral persistence triggers innate and adaptive immune responses in the liver, and chemokines such as CXCL16 help orchestrate the recruitment of immune cells that both contain the virus and injure hepatocytes. The demonstration that this process is governed, at least in part, by promoter methylation adds an epigenetic layer to the known immunopathology of hepatitis B, and it identifies CXCL16 as a novel target for clinical evaluation and intervention. If future work confirms that modulating CXCL16 methylation or expression can influence inflammatory outcomes, the pathway could become more than a passive marker and evolve into a genuine therapeutic axis. Several considerations temper immediate application. The study reports associations in a cross-sectional design, so causality between hypomethylation, chemokine expression and inflammation cannot be fully disentangled from the present data, and longitudinal follow-up would be needed to determine whether CXCL16 promoter methylation predicts disease progression, response to antiviral therapy or the later development of hepatocellular carcinoma. Moreover, methylation patterns can be influenced by age, environment and comorbidities, so the findings will require replication in larger and more diverse cohorts before any routine clinical use. The article was published open access on 14 October 2026 under a Creative Commons licence, and the authors, led by corresponding author Kai Wang, declare no competing interests. Even with those caveats, the convergence of methylation data, gene expression, protein levels and inflammatory correlations in a well-characterised cohort of 217 patients makes a compelling case that an epigenetic signature at the CXCL16 promoter mirrors the inflammatory fires burning in chronically HBV-infected livers, and offers researchers a fresh molecular handle on a disease that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide. A research team at Hiroshima University examined nearly five decades of national viral hepatitis control measures and found that sustained, coordinated policy interventions have substantially reduced the burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, and with it, mortality from hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common form of primary liver cancer. The analysis, led by corresponding authors Junko Tanaka and Tomoyuki Akita, documents an epidemiological transition with direct implications for how Japan, and countries following a similar path, should now prioritize liver cancer prevention. Chronic infection with HBV and HCV has long been recognized as the dominant driver of liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide. Both viruses establish persistent infections in the liver, and over years to decades the resulting chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis create the cellular environment in which malignant transformation becomes increasingly likely. Because the interval between infection and cancer development is so long, the effects of public health interventions targeting viral transmission can take generations to become fully visible in cancer statistics. Japan’s experience offers an unusually clear view of this delayed cascade, because the country implemented systematic countermeasures in successive waves beginning in the 1970s and maintained them through legal, financial, and clinical frameworks into the present decade. The review traces the architecture of Japan’s response in three broad phases. From the 1970s onward, the country focused on blood safety and on reducing healthcare-associated transmission, measures that curtailed two of the most efficient routes of HBV and HCV spread. From 1986 onwards, Japan introduced prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HBV, an intervention with profound intergenerational consequences given that infection at birth carries the highest risk of chronicity. From the 2000s onwards, hepatitis control was institutionalized through dedicated legal and financial frameworks, alongside expanded access to antiviral treatment, allowing large numbers of chronically infected individuals to be identified, monitored, and cured or suppressed. Check Symptoms Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology cancers Cancer cancer To assess the population-level impact of these measures, the researchers searched the PubMed database for peer-reviewed articles related to HCC, liver cancer, viral hepatitis, liver cirrhosis, and Japan published between January 1970 and January 2026. They supplemented this with manual searches of government reports, incorporated data from their own Epidemiological Research Group on Viral Hepatitis and its Long-term Course (VH-Epi), and drew on national vital statistics together with multiple large-scale surveillance and statistics databases. This combination of peer-reviewed literature, official registries, and long-running cohort data allowed the team to reconstruct trends in infection prevalence, incidence, and cancer mortality across the full arc of the national program. Find Cancer Care The prevalence data reveal a striking decline across every population examined. Among first-time blood donors, a group generally regarded as a healthy cross-section of society, the proportion positive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), the marker of active HBV infection, fell from 0.63 percent in 1995–2000 to 0.13 percent in 2017–2021. Over the same period, the proportion positive for HCV antibody, the marker of HCV exposure, fell from 0.49 percent to 0.16 percent. Among residents aged 40 years and older attending health checkups, HBsAg positivity declined from 1.16 percent in 2002 to 0.55 percent in 2021, while anti-HCV positivity fell from 1.16 percent to 0.21 percent. Newly acquired infections in blood donors have reached historically low levels, at 2.38 per 100,000 person-years for HBV and 0.4 per 100,000 person-years for HCV. One of the most consequential findings concerns the youngest generation of mothers. Among pregnant women born in or after 2000, HBsAg-positive individuals have become extremely rare, a pattern Akita attributes directly to the mother-to-child transmission prevention program introduced in 1986. Because chronic HBV infection acquired at birth is the strongest risk factor for lifelong viral persistence and eventual HCC, the near-disappearance of HBsAg positivity in this birth cohort represents an intergenerational protective effect that will continue to propagate through the population as these women and their children age. It illustrates how a single well-targeted intervention, sustained over decades, can reshape the infection landscape for generations that were never directly exposed to the pre-intervention epidemiology. The mortality data tell an equally compelling story. Long-term trends in cancer-specific mortality in Japan between 1958 and 2022 show that liver cancer mortality, which includes both viral-related and non-viral-related disease, rose steadily until the early 2000s and has subsequently declined. This trajectory contrasts sharply with several other major cancers, including pancreatic, lung, and colon cancers, for which mortality has continued to increase over comparable periods. The timing of the liver cancer downturn is consistent with the long natural history of viral hepatitis: the transmission reductions of the 1970s and 1980s, followed by treatment scale-up from the 2000s, have now translated into falling cancer deaths decades later. The proportion of HCC deaths attributed to non-viral causes rose from 6.8 percent in 1992 to 56.0 percent in 2019. The review emphasizes that this shift largely reflects the substantial decline in viral hepatitis-related HCC rather than a comparable increase in the absolute burden of non-viral disease. In other words, the denominator has changed: viral hepatitis no longer dominates the country’s liver cancer mortality, and non-viral etiologies now account for more than half of HCC deaths. The principal non-viral contributors are alcohol-related liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the latter reflecting the growing global prevalence of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome as drivers of chronic liver injury. The transition does not mean the hepatitis problem is solved. The review identifies several high-risk populations in whom viral hepatitis remains an important concern, including persons who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, migrants from regions where HBV is endemic, and incarcerated populations. Reaching these groups with testing, linkage to care, and prevention services remains a central challenge as Japan moves toward the World Health Organization’s 2030 elimination targets, which call for dramatic reductions in new infections and deaths relative to a 2015 baseline. Maintaining the gains already achieved, through continued surveillance, blood safety, vaccination coverage, and treatment access, is described as essential even as the epidemiological center of gravity shifts. The authors frame their findings as transferable lessons for other countries pursuing viral hepatitis elimination. Japan’s experience demonstrates that phased interventions, beginning with transmission control, extending to vertical transmission prevention, and culminating in legally anchored, funded treatment programs, can produce measurable population-level declines in infection prevalence and, with an appropriate time lag, in virus-associated cancer mortality. It also demonstrates that success creates new obligations: as Akita notes, the next step is to achieve and sustain viral hepatitis elimination while adapting liver cancer prevention to the country’s changing disease landscape. For Japan, that means building prevention and early-detection strategies around alcohol-related liver disease and MASLD, while for countries earlier in the elimination pathway, the Japanese trajectory provides both a roadmap and a preview of the epidemiological transition that successful control will eventually bring. records.content: 首页 新闻 军事 汽车 游戏 科技 旅游 经济 娱乐 投资 培训 文化 守艺中华 佛教 红木 韩流 简读 军事APP 头条APP 注册 登录 中华网家电 设为书签Ctrl+D将本页面保存为书签,全面了解最新资讯,方便快捷。 业 界/ 互联网/ 行 业/ 通 信/ 数 码/ 手 机/ 平 板/ 笔记本/ 相 机 当前位置:频道首页 > 快讯 > 正文 乙肝治愈新药会取代现有方案吗?答案可能和你想的不一样! 乙肝治愈新药会取代现有方案吗?答案可能和你想的不一样! 2026-10-12 18:42:04 来源:财讯网 小 大 军事APP头条APP 分享微信 × 用微信扫码二维码 分享至好友和朋友圈 目前,慢乙肝领域已有两款用于实现临床治愈的药物,一款是长效干扰素(商品名:派格宾,通用名:聚乙二醇干扰素α-2b),其于2025年10月在国内获批。另一款是新药贝普若韦生(英文名:Bepirovirsen,研发代号:GSK836),其于2026年8月先在日本获批,国内申请还在推进中。 既然这两种药物都和临床治愈相关,那么它们之间有什么区别呢?我们要不要等新药上市再治?长效干扰素会被新药替代吗?......其实这两种药物有着不同的机制,在乙肝治疗的作用环节也不一样,并不是简单的“谁取代谁”的关系。 01 它们两个的作用机制不同 乙肝病毒会在肝细胞里留下一个复制母版,也就是我们常说的cccDNA,它会不断向外发出生产指令,制造表面抗原等病毒“组件”。这些表面抗原就像病毒放出的烟雾弹,会麻痹免疫系统,让免疫细胞认不出敌人。这里有两个关键点,一是乙肝病毒会不断产生表面抗原,二是高表面抗原会抑制我们的免疫功能。 贝普若韦生是一种反义寡核苷酸(ASO)药物,它可以阻断表面抗原的合成,让血液中的表面抗原降下来,烟雾散开,免疫细胞才重新看得见病毒。也有研究提示它可能有一定先天免疫刺激作用[1],但对临床治愈的具体贡献还不明确。 长效干扰素具有“直接抗病毒+免疫重建”双重机制:能一边抑制病毒复制,一边唤醒被病毒催眠的免疫系统,让免疫细胞识别并清除被感染的肝细胞,并形成长期的免疫记忆,停药之后,免疫细胞也能继续站岗,防止病毒卷土重来[2]。 不难发现,贝普若韦生的特点是快速降低表面抗原,长效干扰素的特点是能重建免疫,形成持久性的免疫控制,解决的是两个不同的问题。 02 两款药物的临床数据对比 先说明,临床治愈也称功能性治愈,是指停止抗病毒治疗24周后,乙肝表面抗原仍检测不到、HBV DNA低于定量下限、伴或不伴表面抗体出现,且相关肝功能指标恢复正常;实现临床治愈后,可以长期停药,肝硬化和肝癌风险也会明显下降[2],但仍需定期复查。 贝普若韦生的优势: 降低表面抗原的速度快 根据II期数据,治疗4周,便能看到表面抗原的快速下降,平均HBsAg下降约1.56 log10IU/mL,数据下降明显[3]。 在治愈率方面,根据其III期临床研究B-Well 1和B-Well 2的结果,在核苷经治、HBsAg 100-3000 IU/mL的患者中,贝普若韦生联合核苷(酸)类药物(NA)的临床治愈率分别为 20%和19%;在HBsAg 100-1000 IU/mL的人群中临床治愈率分别为25%和28%[4]。 其中中国患者总体临床治愈率为24%,HBsAg<1000 IU/mL人群的临床治愈率为35%。 长效干扰素的优势: 持久激活免疫、疗效持久、远期获益明确 治愈率方面,III期研究显示,核苷经治、HBsAg<1500 IU/mL的患者使用长效干扰素联合NA,临床治愈率为31.4%,HBsAg<100 IU/mL的患者能达到66.7%[5]。另一项研究中,HBsAg<3000 IU/mL的患者使用长效干扰素联合恩替卡韦治疗,临床治愈率为27.71%,HBsAg 100-1000 IU/mL人群的临床治愈率为39.53%[6]。 持久性方面,经长效干扰素获得临床治愈后的患者延长随访130周,初治患者治愈维持率100%,核苷经治患者治愈维持率超过85%[7]。 防肝癌方面,接受基于长效干扰素治疗的患者,肝癌发生风险降低约90%,治疗后5年肝癌累积发生率降低至1%左右[8],接近健康人群水平。而贝普若韦生刚上市,这方面的长期数据还需要时间积累。 03 两款药物该怎么选? 答案可能是“都需要” 现有证据表明,要实现持久的临床治愈,需要同时做到两点:一是充分降低表面抗原,解除高抗原对免疫系统的抑制作用;二是帮助身体重新建立起针对乙肝病毒的特异性免疫,进而形成长期的免疫控制,避免停药后复发。 新药贝普若韦生降低表面抗原的速度快,但只靠它难以建立起长期的免疫记忆,停药后容易复发;长效干扰素具有强免疫作用,能帮助身体建立稳固的长期免疫,但如果患者的抗原水平很高,又会在一定程度上影响免疫激活的效率。 两者联用刚好可以优势互补:贝普若韦生把抗原降下来,降低病毒的免疫抑制作用,给免疫系统松绑;长效干扰素把免疫激活起来,形成长期的免疫记忆。二者联合,最终实现更快转阴,更稳停药。这一联用策略已经得到了初步的验证:一项IIb期研究显示,贝普若韦生与聚乙二醇干扰素联用,停药随访24周复阳率为0,明显低于未联用干扰素的方案[9]。 两类药物的对比如下,大家可以保存下来: 04 写在最后 随着医学技术的不断发展,乙肝新药越来越多,大家可以选择的治疗方案也越来越多,但这并不意味着现有方案被否定。能不能追求临床治愈、单药还是联用、按什么顺序治疗,都要由专业医生结合我们的表面抗原水平、肝功能、肝硬度和基础病等综合判断。 此外,贝普若韦生在国内尚未获批,虽然网上流传它24周一个疗程的费用可能在15万-30万元,但尚未证实,最终价格、获批人群,请以官方信息为准。在此之前,不要自行停药、换药,也别盲目找药试药;规范治疗、定期复查,就是眼下最稳妥的选择。 参考文献 [1]Ermler ME, Delahaye JL, Jordan W, et al. records.content: 今日动态 返回首页 会员注册 登录 生物通快讯免费订阅 首页 今日动态 人才市场 新技术专栏 中国科学人 云展台 BioHot 定制我的BioHot 进入我的BioHot 进入我的集采 肿瘤癌症研究 免疫/基因/细胞疗法 神经生物学 健康与疾病 衰老机制与长寿 单细胞技术 基因编辑-CRISPR RNA研究 肠道菌与人体微生态 细胞代谢 AI生物信息学 COVID 云讲堂直播 会展中心 特价专栏 技术快讯 免费试用 生物通官微 陪你抓住生命科技 跳动的脉搏 生物通首页 > 今日动态 > 正文 埃塞俄比亚巴哈达尔市公立医院门诊患者乙型肝炎病毒流行率及其相关因素研究 《Discover Public Health》:Prevalence of hepatitis B virus and associated factors among patients attending outpatient department at public hospitals in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月15日 来源:Discover Public Health 1.3 编辑推荐: 背景:乙型肝炎病毒(Hepatitis B virus, HBV)感染仍然是埃塞俄比亚的一个重大公共卫生问题。本研究旨在确定埃塞俄比亚西北部巴哈达尔市公立医院门诊患者的HBV感染流行率及其相关因素。 方法:研究人员于2026年3月至6月开展了一项基于医院的横断 瑞孚迪自动化解决方案>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 背景:乙型肝炎病毒(Hepatitis B virus, HBV)感染仍然是埃塞俄比亚的一个重大公共卫生问题。本研究旨在确定埃塞俄比亚西北部巴哈达尔市公立医院门诊患者的HBV感染流行率及其相关因素。 方法:研究人员于2026年3月至6月开展了一项基于医院的横断面研究,共纳入422名巴哈达尔市公立医院的门诊就诊者。采用随机起始后的每隔约第二位就诊者的系统抽样法选取参与者。收集社会人口学、行为学和临床数据,并使用SNIBE Maglumi分析仪检测静脉血样本的乙型肝炎表面抗原(HBsAg)。数据采用SPSS 26版进行分析。双变量分析中p < 0.25的变量被纳入多变量逻辑回归分析,p < 0.05视为具有统计学显著性。 结果:HBV流行率为12.32%(95% CI: 9.18–15.46%)。与HBV感染相关的因素包括年龄 ≥ 35岁(调整后优势比AOR = 2.31; 95% CI: 1.01–5.27)、离异/丧偶状态(AOR = 3.14; 95% CI: 1.35–5.80)、未接受正规教育(AOR = 3.04; 95% CI: 1.36–5.62)、黄疸(AOR = 2.84; 95% CI: 1.26–5.21)、深色尿(AOR = 3.25; 95% CI: 2.31–6.14)、右上腹疼痛(AOR = 5.16; 95% CI: 2.83–8.64)、输血史(AOR = 2.45; 95% CI: 1.23–4.71)、共用锐器(AOR = 1.68; 95% CI: 1.04–3.23)、性传播感染(sexually transmitted infections, STI)史(AOR = 3.62; 95% CI: 2.16–5.37)、不使用安全套(AOR = 1.54; 95% CI: 1.06–3.25)以及饮酒(AOR = 2.16; 95% CI: 1.08–3.24)。疫苗接种与较低的感染几率相关(AOR = 0.68; 95% CI: 0.28–0.84)。 结论:在巴哈达尔的门诊就诊者中,HBV感染仍然是一个重大的公共卫生问题。加强疫苗接种、针对性筛查、健康教育、安全性行为实践以及感染预防措施可能有助于减少HBV传播并改善与护理的联系。 研究背景与问题 欢迎领取《CGT 研发全流程解决方案》领 取 乙型肝炎病毒(Hepatitis B virus, HBV)感染是全球主要的公共卫生问题之一,可导致慢性肝病、肝硬化甚至肝细胞癌(hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC)。尽管已有有效疫苗和抗病毒疗法,但在低收入和中等收入国家,尤其是撒哈拉以南非洲地区,HBV的疾病负担依然沉重。埃塞俄比亚属于HBV高流行区,其合并流行率估计在6%至12%之间。然而,针对普通门诊患者这一特定人群的HBV感染证据较为匮乏,尤其是在巴哈达尔市。许多具有可识别风险因素的门诊患者从未接受过HBV筛查。因此,开展此项研究旨在确定巴哈达尔市公立医院门诊患者的HBV感染流行率及其相关因素,为制定和实施有针对性的HBV预防和控制策略提供依据,助力实现到2030年消除病毒性肝炎这一公共卫生威胁的全球目标。 研究方法与关键技术 研究人员于2026年3月至6月在埃塞俄比亚巴哈达尔市的两家公立综合专科医院——Felege Hiwot综合专科医院(FHCSH)和Tibebe Ghion综合专科医院(TGCSH)开展了一项基于医院的横断面研究。研究样本量为422名门诊就诊者,采用按比例分配和系统抽样的方法从两家医院招募参与者。数据通过面对面访谈的结构化问卷收集,涵盖社会人口学特征、行为因素以及医疗和潜在暴露相关因素。实验室检测方面,研究人员采集参与者的静脉血样本,使用SNIBE Maglumi化学发光免疫分析(chemiluminescence immunoassay, CLIA)仪检测乙型肝炎表面抗原(HBsAg)。数据分析采用SPSS 26版软件,通过双变量和多变量逻辑回归分析确定与HBV感染相关的因素。 研究结果 社会人口学、行为学和临床特征 研究共纳入422名参与者,应答率为100%。其中,41%的参与者年龄在25至34岁之间,35%超过35岁,24%低于25岁。婚姻状况方面,49%已婚,25%单身,26%离异或丧偶。51%的受访者报告感到疲劳或虚弱,46%报告右上腹腹痛。28%有输血史,45%曾接受手术或拔牙。近一半(48%)报告共用锐器,42%有住院史。此外,51%报告有性传播感染(STI)史。大多数参与者(70%)未接种HBV疫苗。 HBV感染流行率 研究发现,门诊患者的HBV感染流行率为12.32%(95%置信区间CI: 9.18–15.46%),而370人(87.68%)为阴性。 双变量逻辑回归分析 双变量分析显示,年龄≥35岁(粗优势比COR=2.74; 95% CI: 1.16–6.48; p=0.021)、离异或丧偶状态(COR=3.21; 95% CI: 1.47–7.00; p=0.003)、STI史(COR=3.75; 95% CI: 1.93–7.30; p<0.001)以及饮酒(COR=2.36; 95% CI: 1.25–4.44; p=0.008)与HBV感染显著正相关。HBV疫苗接种显示出强大的保护效应(COR=0.27; 95% CI: 0.11–0.67; p=0.003)。家族HBV史、手术/牙科操作和住院史与HBV感染无显著关联。 与HBV感染相关的因素 多变量逻辑回归分析确定了多个独立相关因素: • 年龄≥35岁的参与者感染HBV的几率是年龄<25岁者的2.31倍(调整后优势比AOR=2.31; 95% CI: 1.01–5.27; p=0.047)。 • 离异或丧偶个体的感染几率是单身者的3.14倍(AOR=3.14; 95% CI: 1.35–5.80; p=0.002)。 • 未接受正规教育的参与者感染几率是有大学及以上学历者的3.04倍(AOR=3.04; 95% CI: 1.36–5.62; p=0.04)。 • 共用锐器与HBV感染显著相关(AOR=1.68; 95% CI: 1.04–3.23; p=0.02)。 • STI史与HBV感染强相关,感染几率增加超过三倍(AOR=3.62; 95% CI: 2.16–5.37; p<0.001)。 • 饮酒与HBV感染显著相关(AOR=2.16; 95% CI: 1.08–3.24; p=0.003)。 • 性行为时不使用安全套使感染几率增加(AOR=1.54; 95% CI: 1.06–3.25; p=0.004)。 • HBV疫苗接种显示出保护作用,接种者感染几率比未接种者低32%(AOR=0.68; 95% CI: 0.28–0.84; p=0.004)。 • 临床表现为黄疸(AOR=2.84; 95% CI: 1.26–5.21)、深色尿(AOR=3.25; 95% CI: 2.31–6.14)和右上腹疼痛(AOR=5.16; 95% CI: 2.83–8.64)也与HBV感染显著相关。 • 输血史同样与感染相关(AOR=2.45; 95% CI: 1.23–4.71)。 讨论与结论 讨论部分指出,本研究中12.32%的HBV流行率表明该地区处于高流行状态,与埃塞俄比亚其他一些门诊患者研究的结果相似或介于不同研究报告的流行率范围之间。研究发现的多个相关因素与其他研究一致:年龄增长与累积暴露风险增加有关;离异/丧偶状态可能伴随高风险行为;低教育水平影响健康素养和预防措施的采纳;临床表现如黄疸、右上腹痛和深色尿是肝损伤的典型体征;输血、共用锐器和STI史证实了血液和性传播途径的重要性;饮酒可能通过行为机制和免疫抑制增加风险。最重要的是,HBV疫苗接种的保护效应再次确认了其在预防感染中的核心地位。 研究的局限性包括横断面设计无法推断因果关系,研究对象局限于公立医院门诊患者,结果不能推广至普通人群或私立医疗机构患者,以及部分行为风险因素数据依赖自我报告可能存在回忆偏倚。 结论部分翻译如下: HBV感染仍是巴哈达尔公立医院门诊就诊者中的一个重要公共卫生问题,其流行率表明该地区处于高流行状态。观察到的与HBV感染相关的因素,包括社会人口学特征、临床表现、行为习惯和医疗相关暴露,强调了采取综合性、有针对性的HBV预防和控制策略的必要性。加强疫苗接种、针对性筛查和早期诊断、健康教育、安全性行为实践以及医疗机构内的感染预防措施,可能有助于减少HBV传播并改善与适当护理的联系。这些努力对于教育资源有限的人群以及其他HBV相关风险因素暴露增加的群体尤为重要,并将有助于推动实现世界卫生组织(WHO)消除肝炎的目标。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! 从2000到2026,27载全因有您;您的每一分支持,都给予我们无穷的动力! 公测期:打赏8元解锁30天免费阅读! 下载安捷伦电子书《通过细胞代谢揭示新的药物靶点》探索如何通过代谢分析促进您的药物发现研究 10x Genomics新品Visium HD 开启单细胞分辨率的全转录组空间分析! 欢迎下载Twist《不断变化的CRISPR筛选格局》电子书 下载《细胞内蛋白质互作分析方法电子书》 引领行业 | 聚焦麦特绘谱代谢组学整体解决方案>> 「大小鼠繁育与健康管理」指导海报,点击即可免费领取电子版或实体海报>> 揭秘单细胞测序-深入了解这项正在改变我们开展科学研究的技术>> 世界著名Thermo Fisher赛默飞世尔科技招聘Field Application Scientist、Marketing Develop等职位,详情请查看生物通人才市场栏目!>> 相关新闻 生物通微信公众号 生物通新浪微博 微信 新浪微博 我要投稿 搜索 国际 国内 人物 产业 热点 科普 热搜:乙型肝炎病毒|流行率|相关因素|门诊患者|埃塞俄比亚|横断面研究 热点排行 1机器学习力场揭示锂离子电池电解液中的多锂离子簇聚现象 2全球保护区域覆盖面积显著超过当前估计:基于25个国家和地区代表性样本对GBF Target 3陆地覆盖进展的重新评估 3髓系选择性IL-10受体激动剂:基于TYK2依赖性与受体几何构象的细胞类型选择性细胞因子信号工程 4Elp1 是髓系分化和脑细胞回补所必需的 5利用化学诱导产生的全能干细胞来模拟小鼠胚胎发生过程 6竞争机制使bcc二元及中熵合金在20 K下增韧 7IDH突变胶质瘤中星形细胞瘤与少突胶质细胞瘤的基因组分化演化:驱动事件、突变特征与治疗选择压力 今日动态 | 人才市场 | 新技术专栏 | 中国科学人 | 云展台 | BioHot | 云讲堂直播 | 会展中心 | 特价专栏 | 技术快讯 | 免费试用 版权所有 生物通 Copyright© eBiotrade.com, All Rights Reserved 联系信箱: 粤ICP备09063491号

Advertisement Human Intestine Concept Featuring Microvilli Surface, Capillaries, H. pylori Bacteria Credit: Adobe Images Approximately 2.3 million new cases of cancer worldwide in 2024, or 1 in 8 of all new cases, were attributable to an infection, in the first global analysis to include HIV in an estimate of cancer incidence from infection.1 Most of the infections were preventable, according to the report, or could have been treated before cancer develops. "Infectious agents are a major preventable cause of cancer globally and are estimated to be the leading modifiable risk factor for cancer among women in 141 countries and men in 58 countries," observe Harriet Rumgay, PhD, Cancer Surveillance Branch, International Agency for Research on Cancer, Lyon, France, and colleagues. "Importantly, many carcinogenic infectious agents have existing or potential preventive interventions, including vaccines, diagnostics, treatments, and safe-injection practices." The investigators note that 13 infectious agents—including 9 viruses, one bacterium and 3 parasites—are categorized as Group 1 carcinogens in humans in the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Monographs Progamme.2 These include Helicobacter pylori, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), human papillomavirus (HPV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and Kaposi's sacroma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). These pathogens are implicated in 37 causal infection-cancer pairs, including: from H pylori, non-cardia gastric cancer, cardia gastric cancer, and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma of gastric location from HBV, hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma from KSHV, Kaposi's sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma Drawing on the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today (GLOBOCAN) database of cancer incidence in 2024, Rumgay and colleagues estimated the population-attributable fraction (PAF), absolute numbers, and age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR) of new cancer cases attributable to 12 of the infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up The largest number of cases was attributable to H pylori (n=760,000; PAF 4%); followed by HPV (n=750,000, 4%), EBV (n=260,000, 1%) HCV (n=160,000, <1%) and KSHV (n=35,000, <1%). The corresponding ASIR for all infections combined was 22.7 cancer cases per 100,000 person-years.HPV had the highest ASIR for infection-attributable cases (7.7), followed by H pylori (6.9), HBV (3.4), EBV (2.6), HCV (1.5) and KSHV (0.4). The investigators found the largest number of infection-attributable cancer cases in eastern Asia (999,000 cases, 42% of global total); with the region having a PAF of 15% and an ASIR of 31.9 per 100,000 person-years.Other regions with higher PAFs and ASIRs than the global average included sub-Saharan Africa, central and Eastern Europe and southeastern Asia. Rumgay and colleagues point out that despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a global challenge, "with persistent inequities especially impacting low-income and middle-income countries." What You Need to Know About 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, or 1 in 8 of all new cases, were attributable to infection, according to the first global analysis to include HIV in its estimate. Helicobacter pylori (760,000 cases) and HPV (750,000 cases) caused the largest share of infection-attributable cancers, and eastern Asia carried the heaviest regional burden, with 42% of the global total. Because most of these infections can be prevented or treated before cancer develops, the investigators call for wider access to HPV vaccination, H pylori screen-and-treat programs, and long-acting injectable HIV PrEP, especially in low- and middle-income countries. They point to H pylori as a major cause of cancer globally, despite improved sanitation programs and reduced incidence of intrafamilial transmissions. They recognize several recent initiatives to address the persistently high incidence, however, including population-based gastric cancer screening endoscopy programs in Japan, South Korea and China; and H pylori "screen-and-treat” programs in several countries in Europe. With the direct association of cervical cancer to HPV, Rumgay and colleagues urge greater access to HPV vaccine in low- and middle-income countries, "if increasing inequalities in future cervical cancer burden are to be avoided". Noting that HIV-attributable cancer burden is highest in southern and eastern Africa, the investigators commend the 2025 WHO approval of long-acting, injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis. PrEP holds great potential for primary prevention by reducing HIV transmission and HIV attributable cancers, they indicate, "if integrated into a comprehensive combination approach spanning condom promotion, HIV testing, and harm reduction services for people who inject drugs." The study was characterized as a "staggering new analysis" in one health center press release, in which medical faculty emphasized that preventable infections are a substantial but often overlooked cause of cancer.3 "This recent Lancet data is a profound reminder that a significant portion of our global cancer burden is fundamentally preventable," stated David Greenberg, MD, Hematology Oncology, Hackensack Meridian Health, Neptune, New Jersey."We have historically siloed infectious diseases and oncology, but they are deeply intertwined.By shifting toward aggressive infection control, we can literally vaccinate and treat our way out of millions of future cancer diagnoses." A third dose of HepB-CpG vaccine may improve immunoprotection among individuals with HIV. NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Two doses of hepatitis B virus vaccine with CpG adjuvant may not be sufficient for people with HIV who do not respond to an initial vaccination series, according to a poster presentation at ACG Annual Scientific Meeting. Data from pooled analysis did not show statistically significant superiority between two doses of HepB-CpG (Heplisav-B, Dynavax) compared with three doses of HBV vaccine with an aluminum-based adjuvant (Engenrix-B, GSK; Recombivax HB, Merck). “For a person with HIV who did not respond to a prior hepatitis B series, HepB-CpG is the preferred revaccination choice over the old alum vaccines, and a third dose is worth considering when durable, high-level protection is the goal,” Mexan Mapouka, MD, MPH, an internal medicine resident at University of Maryland Capital Region Health, told Healio. “The take-home is not ‘the vaccines are equal,’ but rather ‘two doses may not be enough for everyone.’ So check titers and consider a third dose, which lines up with what current HIV and opportunistic-infection guidelines already recommend.” People with HIV are less likely to achieve serologic response to conventional HBV vaccines, according to study background. Two or three doses of HepB-CpG have been recommended for nonresponders in this patient population. However, it remains relatively unknown whether three doses of HepB-CpG, rather than two, provide adequate protection compared with the three doses of the aluminum-based vaccines. “Guidelines now point toward the newer adjuvanted vaccine HepB-CpG for these patients, but they were not settled on whether two doses is enough for prior nonresponders or whether a third dose is needed to match or beat the old three-dose alum vaccines,” Mapouka said. “The study set out to pool the available data and try to answer that practical, everyday question.” Mapouka and colleagues conducted a systematic and meta-analysis comprised of research published through Jan. 24. Analysis included 493 individuals (mean age, 45 years; 46% white), most of whom were men. The group was balanced in receipt of HepB-CpG (n = 248) and HepB-alum (n = 245) vaccines. Pooled analysis did not show a statistically significant difference in seroconversion with the two-dose HepB-CpG regimen, with no clear superiority observed (RR = 1.35; 95% CI, 0.97-1.87), even with high heterogeneity (I2 = 86.5%). Seroprotection was lower than the 90% threshold among those with diabetes (70.2%) and smokers (84%), according to subgroup analyses. Optimizing CD4 levels could boost HBV antibody response in these subgroups, the researchers noted. “The most useful future studies would be larger head-to-head trials that enroll more patients with low CD4 counts, who are underrepresented so far; follow antibody titers for several years to measure real durability rather than early response; and look at host factors like diabetes, smoking and inflammation to see who needs an extra dose or other help,” Mapouka told Healio. “Measuring T-cell responses, not just antibodies, would also add value, since T-cell immunity is impaired in HIV even when antibodies look adequate.” For more information: Mexan Mapouka, MD, MPH, can be reached at mexan.mapouka@umm.edu. Advertisement Updated: 2:02 PM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says Updated: 2:02 PM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN CNN — Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether. That's according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology , which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments. Advertisement Related video above | Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment "We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer," said Gary Clifford, the study's senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. "We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works," Clifford said. "It's an awareness-raising issue." About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024. Other infections contributed substantially as well: Hepatitis B or HBV was linked to an estimated 360,000 cancer cases, which were mostly liver cancers. The Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV, was associated with about 260,000 cancer cases, of which a head and neck cancer starting in the nasopharynx was the main driver. Hepatitis C or HCV was tied to 160,000 cancer cases, mostly liver cancers. "Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development," Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email. "However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV," Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available. Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set. The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018 , but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV. "EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma," Clifford said. "That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we've identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas," he said. "We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn't really fully addressed because we didn't understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing." Where the infection-related cancer burden is greatest The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn't evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment. But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives. "Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later," said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study. "Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States," she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV. "Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer," Fedirko said. "Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures." How to 'take away' the risk Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference. Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops. Getting tested and following up with a doctor "almost takes away any cancer risk," Clifford said. Once infections get diagnosed, "we know how to manage them," he said. "The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we're learning more about which ones, but that's a work in progress. The point is: It doesn't mean that you've got a cancer just because you have the infection." For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road. The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop. Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection. HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses , which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer : cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection. The new research "teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer," Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email. "This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced," Lee said. "Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower." Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include "safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis," Rumgay said. "If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide." IIa Study 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月14日 来源:LIVER INTERNATIONAL 6.2 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Open Access 背景与目的:慢性乙型肝炎(CHB)仍是一项重大的全球健康负担。由于乙型肝炎表面抗原(HBsAg)清除率低、病毒复制模板——共价闭合环状DNA(cccDNA)持续存在,以及需要终身治疗,当前疗法很少能实现功能性治愈。GST-HG131是一种首创的、可口服生物利用的PAPD5/7小分子抑制剂,PAPD5/7是参与HBV mRNA稳定化和HBsAg产生的关键宿主因子。研究人员在一项随机、双盲、安慰剂对照的IIa期研究中,评估了GST-HG131在接受核苷(酸)类似物(NUC)治疗的CHB患者中的安全性、耐受性和抗病毒活性。 方法:这项双盲、随机、安慰剂对照的IIa期研究评估了GST-HG131在45例CHB患者中的疗效和安全性。队列1和队列2(各n=10;8例活性药物、2例安慰剂)分别接受30 mg或60 mg每日两次(BID)治疗28天。队列3(n=25;20例活性药物、5例安慰剂)接受30 mg BID治疗12周。所有参与者均接受核苷(酸)类似物单药治疗超过6个月,HBsAg水平在100~1500 IU/mL之间,血清丙氨酸氨基转移酶(ALT)低于1×正常值上限(ULN)。 结果:第28天时,30 mg BID 28天组和60 mg BID 28天组的HBsAg降幅分别为?0.65 log 10 IU/mL和?0.53 log 10 IU/mL。30 mg BID 12周组在治疗结束时较安慰剂组显示出更大的降低幅度,为?0.89 log 10 IU/mL(p < 0.001)。三分之二接受治疗的患者实现了HBsAg降低>50%,最大降幅为1.64 log 10 IU/mL。值得注意的是,12周组中76.5%的患者实现了HBsAg低于100 IU/mL。停药后观察到HBsAg反弹。GST-HG131耐受性良好,所有队列中均未观察到剂量相关毒性或新出现的安全性问题。 结论:GST-HG131作为首创的口服PAPD5/7抑制剂,在CHB患者中表现出良好的安全性和显著的HBsAg降低。治疗12周后观察到最强的抗病毒活性,支持GST-HG131作为CHB功能性治愈策略组成部分的进一步临床开发。 试验注册:ClinicalTrials.gov标识符:NCT06263959。 慢性乙型肝炎(CHB)仍是一项全球性重大健康负担,影响超过2.5亿人,是肝硬化和肝细胞癌(HCC)的重要病因。当前一线治疗包括干扰素和核苷(酸)类似物(NUC),虽能有效抑制HBV DNA复制,但难以实现功能性治愈,主要因为乙型肝炎表面抗原(HBsAg)清除率低、病毒复制模板共价闭合环状DNA(cccDNA)持续存在,且多数患者需终身治疗。GST-HG131是一种首创的、可口服生物利用的PAPD5/7小分子抑制剂,通过抑制宿主PAPD5/7酶,促进HBV mRNA降解,从而减少HBsAg产生。本研究旨在评估GST-HG131在NUC抑制治疗下的CHB患者中的安全性、耐受性及抗病毒活性,为功能性治愈策略提供概念验证。 义翘神州通用型Whitlow 218 Linker兔单抗,高效助力CAR流式检测,欢迎索取详细资料>> 领 取 研究人员开展了一项随机、双盲、安慰剂对照的IIa期临床试验,在中国4个中心纳入45例CHB患者。所有患者均接受稳定NUC单药治疗≥6个月,HBsAg为100~1500 IU/mL,ALT低于1×ULN,且为HBeAg阴性。试验设三个队列:队列1接受GST-HG131 30 mg每日两次(BID)28天(8例活性、2例安慰剂),队列2接受60 mg BID 28天(8例活性、2例安慰剂),队列3接受30 mg BID 12周(20例活性、5例安慰剂)。主要终点为HBsAg较基线的变化,采用混合效应重复测量模型(MMRM)分析;同时评估药代动力学(PK)参数和安全性。研究方案经中国人民解放军总医院第五医学中心伦理委员会批准,并在ClinicalTrials.gov注册。 3.1 基线特征 records.content: Health Matters Weekdays · The latest health news and expert advice on living well. Thank you for signing up! Cancer can seem random. It’s often the result of many factors, including genetic mutations that build up over a lifetime of exposure to sun, pollution, and other sources of DNA damage, combined with a person’s genetic predisposition. DNA damage accumulated over time can weaken the body’s ability to suppress out-of-control cell growth, which is how tumors form. But infections are another significant cause of cancer. Uncovering the links between certain infections and cancers raises the hope that by preventing infection, one could prevent certain malignancies. A recent report from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) published in the Lancet Oncology found that 12% of new cancer cases in 2024—the most recent year for which data were available—were caused by 12 infections. Which infections are associated with cancer? Certain human papillomaviruses, or HPV, are behind the majority of cervical cancers and a number of head and neck cancers as well, says Harriet Rumgay, an epidemiologist at IARC who is an author of the new report. About 4% of new cancer diagnoses in 2024 could be attributed to HPV infection. Doctors and researchers have known for decades that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections also drive many cases of liver cancer, linked to 2% and less than 1% of new diagnoses respectively, according to the report. There is also strong evidence linking Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach and small intestine, with gastric cancers. This infection was calculated to be behind about 4% of new diagnoses. And Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), which causes mononucleosis and affects more than 90% of the world’s population, was involved in around 1% of new diagnoses, including lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancers, and gastric cancers. Seven other infections, including HIV, were also flagged as carcinogens in the study. Most people who have these infections will not develop cancer. It’s not also immediate—there may be a years-long delay. And infection is often only one of a number of factors contributing to a given cancer. For instance, when it comes to the relatively high rates of EBV-driven nasopharyngeal cancers in China, researchers believe that some genetic predisposition and environmental factors are also involved. Why do some infections cause cancer? It depends on the infection. In the case of HIV, the virus suppresses the immune system, making it easier for other carcinogenic viruses to replicate. H. pylori causes tissue damage and produces toxins that destabilize the body’s natural control of cellular growth and division, which can lead to cancer. With EBV, says Claire Shannon-Lowe, a virologist at the University of Birmingham in the U.K. who studies EBV and cancer but was not involved in the research, it has to do with how the virus hides within immune cells called B cells. “It's a whole host of things that the virus itself is doing to the B cell to make it continually grow,” she says. That includes blocking normal cellular housecleaning procedures that would both root the virus out and arrest cancer development. How can these cancers be prevented? Some of these infections have treatments. H. pylori can be cleared with antibiotics, for example, reducing the risk of gastric cancer, and treating HIV reduces cancer risk from the infection as well. Some other infections on the list have vaccines. In fact, for some of these vaccines, cancer prevention was a major goal driving their development. “The hepatitis B virus vaccine was the first vaccine that was developed against cancer,” says Rumgay. Likewise, the HPV vaccine, which was approved 20 years ago, is intended to prevent cervical cancer. Cancer epidemiologists may start seeing the effects of widespread HPV vaccination in future analyses, Rumgay says. “More and more people who have been vaccinated are starting to reach the age where we would potentially see the impact on cervical cancer rates or other cancer rates,” she says. However, these vaccines aren’t making it to everyone who might benefit from them. In the U.S., hepatitis B vaccination rates in newborns have declined steeply over the last two years. For other infections, no vaccines are available. For EBV, a nearly ubiquitous virus with a long, clearly documented history of contributing to cancer, “we don't have an effective vaccine yet, or an effective way of preventing it,” says Rumgay. “This is something that we want to highlight with our study.” Historically, it was difficult to interest pharmaceutical companies in vaccines for viruses like EBV that are common and nonlethal, says Lawrence Young, a virologist and emeritus professor of molecular oncology at University of Warwick in the U.K. who has spent his career studying cancer and EBV. (Young was not involved in the IARC research.) But thanks in part to research suggesting EBV might be involved in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disorder, “they've all become very interested,” he says. A number of vaccine candidates are now being studied, with some in clinical trials. For some of the infections implicated by the latest study—the Kaposi-sarcoma associated herpes virus, in particular—there’s need for much more research into prevention, says Rumgay. The hope is that “these new findings might stimulate more development in that area,” she says

Log in A surprising number of cancer cases are tied to common everyday virus and scientists are shedding light on ways people can stay safe. More than 12 percent of global cancer cases are linked to viruses, bacteria and other infections, new research published this year shows. The largest contributors to the disease are Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B virus, Epstein–Barr virus and hepatitis C virus, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer. These infectious agents attack the stomach, genitals, liver, nose and throat. That, in turns, leads to long-term changes in cells making them cancerous. But experts point out that a lot of these infections are preventable using vaccines, or treatable in other ways. “We have very actionable targets,” Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and one of the authors of the research, told The Washington Post on Wednesday. “We have very many tools against these viruses already.” open image in gallery One in eight global cancer cases are linked to viruses and other infections. Experts say there are ways people can reduce or prevent risk (Getty Images) H. pylori Helicobacter pylori, or H. pylori, infects the lining of the stomach and is linked to stomach cancer. The bacteria primarily spreads from person to person, when sharing utensils, shaking hands or other methods of contact with vomit or poop from an infected person. H. pylori can also be passed through contaminated food and water. Ensuring you’re drinking clean water and washing your hands for 20 seconds with soap and water before eating and after using the bathroom can keep you safe, according to the Cleveland Clinic. There’s currently no vaccine for these infections. open image in gallery Scientists say there are may ways to protect yourself from the virus that have been tied to cancer cases (AFP via Getty Images) HPV Human papillomavirus, or HPV, is spread through sexual and non-sexual skin-to-skin contact. People may not know they are infected before passing the virus to their partner. Infections can cause cancer in the penis, anus, vagina, cervix, vulva and the back of the throat. More than 42 million Americans have an active HPV infection, according to the Centers for Disease Control. Fortunately, there is a vaccine for HPV that protects against nine strains of HPV. It’s called Gardasil-9. It’s recommended that people get two doses of the vaccine starting at age 11, according to the CDC. The second dose is administered between six months and a year after the first shot. “HPV vaccines can prevent more than 90 percent of HPV cancers when given at the recommended ages,” the American Cancer Society says. Hepatitis B Hepatitis B is a serious liver infection that can lead to liver cancer. For those who are infected, treatment depends on if its accurate or chronic hepatitis B. Some get medicine, while others need a full on liver transplant. It is estaimted that around 2 billion in the world have had hepatitis B at some point in their life, with roughly 250 million people living with the chronic condition. This virus is also prevented with a vaccine. A series of two-to-three shots is recommended for people starting at infancy, the CDC says. The shots are doled out in six-month increments. Epstein-Barr Epstein-Barr is a common virus that can cause cancer in the nose and throat. The virus spreads through saliva and bodily fluids; that could mean through a kiss, a cough, a sneeze, sexual contact and sharing or touching items that are infected. There is no vaccine to prevent the Epstein-Barr virus yet - though researchers are working on it. Seattle cancer scientists have developed an antibody to block infections in mice. open image in gallery HPV and Hepatitis B infections can be prevented with vaccines, but if they aren’t prevented they can lead to cancers (AFP via Getty Images) People can protect themselves from this virus by avoiding sources of exposure, such as food and drinks or toothbrushes. Washing your hands after touching an infected item, not kissing someone with the virus and using protection when having sex with someone who has the virus can also reduce risk, the Clinic advises. Hepatitis C Hepatitis C is a top cause of liver cancer. There’s no vaccine to prevent Hepatitis C, either, though researchers have been working on it for decades, according to the Mayo Clinic. Fortunately, there are pills that can get rid of the virus in most people who are diagnosed with it. But preventing infection is still the best way to stay safe. Hepatitis C is spread through contact with infected blood, including at birth, during sex and when getting a tattoo or body piercing in an unlicensed facility, according to the CDC. Not sharing needles, getting a blood transfusion or organ transplant from a person who is infected, engaging in sexual activity with a person with the virus, or getting tattoos or piercings at these places can lessen risk, the agency says. Advertisement Updated: 2:02 PM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says Updated: 2:02 PM EDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN CNN — Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether. That's according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology , which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments. Advertisement Related video above | Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment "We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer," said Gary Clifford, the study's senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. "We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works," Clifford said. "It's an awareness-raising issue." About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024. Other infections contributed substantially as well: Hepatitis B or HBV was linked to an estimated 360,000 cancer cases, which were mostly liver cancers. The Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV, was associated with about 260,000 cancer cases, of which a head and neck cancer starting in the nasopharynx was the main driver. Hepatitis C or HCV was tied to 160,000 cancer cases, mostly liver cancers. "Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development," Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email. "However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV," Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available. Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set. The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018 , but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV. "EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma," Clifford said. "That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we've identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas," he said. "We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn't really fully addressed because we didn't understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing." Where the infection-related cancer burden is greatest The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn't evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment. But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives. "Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later," said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study. "Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States," she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV. "Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer," Fedirko said. "Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures." How to 'take away' the risk Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference. Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops. Getting tested and following up with a doctor "almost takes away any cancer risk," Clifford said. Once infections get diagnosed, "we know how to manage them," he said. "The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we're learning more about which ones, but that's a work in progress. The point is: It doesn't mean that you've got a cancer just because you have the infection." For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road. The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop. Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection. HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses , which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer : cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection. The new research "teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer," Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email. "This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced," Lee said. "Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower." Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include "safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis," Rumgay said. "If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide." A comprehensive worldwide analysis evaluating twelve oncogenic pathogens established that infectious agents remain a major preventable cause of cancer morbidity. While overall global age-standardized incidence reached 22.7 cases per 100,000 person-years, low-income and middle-income regions bore more than three-quarters of the entire disease burden. Eastern Asia recorded the largest absolute caseload with 990,000 cases, while sub-Saharan Africa demonstrated the highest proportional impact, where pathogens drove a quarter of all diagnosed malignancies. Pathogen Distribution in Infection-Attributable Cancer. Two primary pathogens drove nearly two-thirds of the total infectious oncologic burden. Helicobacter pylori accounted for 760,000 cases, primarily causing non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma and related gastrointestinal cancer sequelae. Human papillomavirus followed closely with 750,000 cases, responsible for all 600,000 cases of cervical cancer alongside substantial fractions of anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal malignancies. Hepatitis B virus contributed 360,000 cases, predominantly hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Epstein-Barr virus generated 260,000 cases, emerging as the fourth leading pathogen due to established links with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, gastric adenocarcinoma, and diverse lymphoma subtypes. Hepatitis C virus generated 160,000 malignancies. Additional oncogenic agents included Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, Merkel cell polyomavirus, Schistosoma haematobium, liver flukes, and HIV. Clinical Priorities and Infection Control. Managing infection-attributable cancer requires aggressive primary prevention alongside expanded diagnostic screening across primary care systems. Proven tools such as routine immunization against human papillomavirus and hepatitis B yield substantial risk reductions when widely implemented. Early detection of gastric precursors through screen-and-treat protocols for bacterial infection offers measurable clinical efficacy, mirroring successful endoscopic protocols in East Asia. Expanding access to direct-acting antivirals for viral hepatitis, promoting barrier protection, and providing long-acting pre-exposure prophylaxis for populations vulnerable to retroviral transmission further curb oncogenic progression. Clinicians must maintain heightened vigilance regarding oncogenic infectious etiologies, integrating vaccination status reviews and targeted pathogen screening into standard preventive adult care. By shifting our focus toward aggressive infection control, we can literally vaccinate and treat our way out of millions of future cancer diagnoses." One example is H. pylori, or Helicobacter pylori, a common bacterial infection that can lead to stomach cancer and has also been linked to an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The infection can spread through saliva or contaminated food and water. It is treatable with antibiotics and medications that reduce stomach acid. Researchers estimated that 760,000 cancer cases worldwide were attributable to H. pylori, making it the leading infection-related cause of cancer in the study. Infectious disease specialist Alex Lazo-Vasquez, M.D., added that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections can go unnoticed for decades before eventually leading to liver cancer. HPV is another major contributor. The virus can cause several cancers, including cervical cancer in women and penile cancer in men. "Fortunately, we have the tools to protect ourselves. Hepatitis B and HPV are vaccine-preventable, and hepatitis C is now curable with a short course of antiviral medication," Lazo-Vasquez said. "Unfortunately, we are still losing lives to cancers that could potentially be prevented because we are not prioritizing early viral screening and vaccination."
